facts.statement: Jiangxisuchus lived during the Late Cretaceous, specifically the Maastrichtian stage.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Cretaceous: Maastrichtian,

facts.statement: When described in 2019, Jiangxisuchus was initially proposed to be a basal member of the group Crocodyloidea.
facts.quote: At the time of its description in 2019 it was proposed to be a basal member of Crocodyloidea.

facts.statement: A concurrent 2019 study placed Jiangxisuchus in the clade Orientalosuchina, suggesting it was an early alligatoroid.
facts.quote: However, another concurrent 2019 study recovered Jiangxisuchus instead placed it in the clade Orientalosuchina, which were proposed to be early alligatoroids.

facts.statement: The scientific classification of Jiangxisuchus has remained uncertain since its initial description.
facts.quote: The classification of Jiangxisuchus has since then remained in flux.

facts.statement: Jiangxisuchus was a small to medium-sized crocodylian with a short, blunt snout.
facts.quote: Like other orientalosuchins, Jiangxisuchus was a small to medium-sized animal with a short, blunt snout.

facts.statement: Jiangxisuchus was described in 2019 by Chun Li, Xiao-Chun Wu, and Scott James Rufolo as the first crocodilian found in the Cretaceous Nanxiong Formation of Nankang, China.
facts.quote: Jiangxisuchus was described in 2019 by Chun Li, Xiao-Chun Wu and Scott James Rufolo as the first crocodilian from the Cretaceous Nanxiong Formation of Nankang, China.

facts.statement: The name Jiangxisuchus combines the Jiangxi Province of China with the Greek suffix -suchus, meaning crocodile.
facts.quote: The name Jiangxisuchus derives from the Jiangxi Province of eastern China where Nankang is located, combined with the Greek suffix -suchus which translates to crocodile.

facts.statement: Jiangxisuchus had a short and blunt snout similar to that of the extinct genus Stangerochampsa.
facts.quote: Like other orientalosuchins Jiangxisuchus possessed a short and blunt snout, which was initially likened to that of Stangerochampsa.

facts.statement: A prominent notch in the snout contributes to the pronounced festooning, or sinuous appearance, of the jaw in Jiangxisuchus.
facts.quote: This notch also contributes to the pronounced festooning of the jaw, the sinuous appearance of the dental margin created by convex and concave regions across the premaxilla and maxilla.

facts.statement: Jiangxisuchus had large eyesockets with raised rims that were larger than any other openings on its skull.
facts.quote: The eyesockets of Jiangxisuchus were large, larger than any other of the skull openings, had raised rims and may have been topped by palpebrals.

facts.statement: The lower jaw of Jiangxisuchus met at a relatively short symphysis formed entirely by dentary bones, ending just after the fifth tooth socket.
facts.quote: The mandibular symphysis, the region of the two halves of the lower jaw meet each other, is entirely formed by the dentaries to the exclusion of the splenial and described as being relatively short, ending just after the fifth tooth socket.

facts.statement: In the upper jaw, the third premaxillary tooth was the largest, while the first was the smallest.
facts.quote: Of the premaxillary teeth, the third was the largest, with the fourth and fifth being successively smaller and the first the smallest.

facts.statement: The fifth maxillary tooth was the largest in the upper jaw, followed by the fourth and eleventh.
facts.quote: In the maxillary toothrow, the fifth is the largest tooth, followed by the fourth and eleventh.

facts.statement: The first nine upper teeth were conical, unserrated, and slightly curved.
facts.quote: The upper jaw features two different tooth morphologies, with those in the premaxilla and the first nine maxillary teeth all being conical, unserrated and with a slight curvature to them.

facts.statement: From the tenth tooth onward, the upper teeth had constricted bases and low, bean-shaped crowns.
facts.quote: This changes with the tenth tooth, from which onward the teeth have a constricted base and low, bean-shaped crowns.

facts.statement: The lower jaw of Jiangxisuchus contained 19 teeth in total.
facts.quote: The lower jaw contained 19 teeth in total, with the preserved fourth tooth sharing its morphology with the fifth maxillary tooth.

facts.statement: The fourth lower tooth was the largest, and the twelfth was likely the second largest.
facts.quote: As is usual, the fourth dentary tooth is the largest of the lower jaw and alveolar size indicates that the twelfth would have been the second largest.

facts.statement: Bony septums separated some lower jaw teeth, and a gap existed between the eighth and ninth lower teeth.
facts.quote: There are several partial or complete bony septums that separate some of the teeth of the lower jaw and a diastema is present between the eighth and ninth dentary teeth.

facts.statement: The bite mechanism showed an overbite near the front of the upper jaw and interlocking teeth between the seventh and eighth maxillary teeth.
facts.quote: Occlusal pits are present medial to the first two premaxillary teeth, indicating an overbite in that region, but between the seventh and eight maxillary teeth, indicating interlocking of the teeth there.

facts.statement: Evidence suggests Jiangxisuchus had armored limbs, indicated by an elliptical osteoderm lacking a crest.
facts.quote: Among the osteoderms is a single eliptical piece that lacks a crest. This would suggest that the osteoderm would in life have been part of the appendicular armor, meaning Jiangxisuchus had armored limbs.

facts.statement: Jiangxisuchus was a small to medium-sized animal, consistent with a trend among orientalosuchins.
facts.quote: Jiangxisuchus is described as small to medium sized, something that appears to have been a trend among orientalosuchins.

facts.statement: Scientists disagree on whether Jiangxisuchus is a crocodyloid or an alligatoroid and its exact relationship to orientalosuchins.
facts.quote: The classification of Jiangxisuchus has changed repeatedly since its description, with studies disagreeing over whether or not Jiangxisuchus is a crocodyloid or an alligatoroid and its precise relationship with orientalosuchins.

facts.statement: Some studies place Jiangxisuchus as the closest relative to the early Paleocene species Eoalligator chunyii.
facts.quote: In this position, the animal was furthermore recovered as the sister taxon to the early Paleocene Eoalligator chunyii.

facts.statement: Later studies still found Jiangxisuchus and Eoalligator to be sister taxa, though the rest of the group's relationships shifted.
facts.quote: By the description of the latter relationships had shifted slightly, with Krabisuchus and Protoalligator in basal positions, Orientalosuchus, Dongnanosuchus and Eurycephalosuchus in a polytomy and finally Jiangxisuchus and Eoalligator still as sister taxa.

facts.statement: While many studies group Jiangxisuchus with Orientalosuchina as early alligatoroids, this classification is contested.
facts.quote: However while multiple papers have recovered Jiangxisuchus as a member of a monophyletic Orientalosuchina at the base of alligatoroidea, this view is not uncontested.

facts.statement: A 2021 study by Rio and Manion classified Jiangxisuchus as an early crocodyloid rather than an alligatoroid.
facts.quote: One example for this a study published by Jonathan P. Rio and Phillip D. Manion in 2021, in which Jiangxisuchus is an early branching crocodyloid diverging just before the split between Crocodylidae and Mekosuchinae.

facts.statement: In conflicting studies, Jiangxisuchus was consistently found to be closer to crocodiles and gharials than to alligatoroids.
facts.quote: Regardless of the precise plament of Orientalosuchina (once as basal longirostrans and once as early alligatoroids), Jiangxisuchus was recovered as being closer to Longirostres (crocodiles and gharials) than alligatoroids in both instances.

facts.statement: A 2023 study by Ristevski et al. proposed an intermediate classification placing Jiangxisuchus within the Australian group Mekosuchinae.
facts.quote: An intermediate between the crocodyloid interpretation and the Orientalosuchina classification has been recovered by Jorgo Ristevski and colleagues in 2023, though it simultaneously added yet another competing topology into the mix.

facts.statement: The hypothesis that Orientalosuchina belongs within Mekosuchinae has weak support due to few shared unique traits.
facts.quote: However this view is likewise not without caveats and the support for Orientalosuchina being placed within Mekosuchinae remains weak.

facts.statement: Jiangxisuchus lived in a subhumid environment near the base of an alluvial fan influenced by rivers.
facts.quote: The Hekou Formation is marked by the influence of rivers and is thought to have been deposited in a subhumid environment in the proximal parts of an alluvial fan.

facts.statement: The geological age of the Hekou Formation, where Jiangxisuchus fossils were found, is typically accepted as Maastrichtian, though some studies suggest a range from Coniacian to Santonian.
facts.quote: The age of the Hekou Formation is typically accepted to be Maastrichtian, though some studies have considered a Coniacian to Santonian age as well.

facts.statement: Jiangxisuchus belongs to the crocodilian group Longirostres.
facts.quote: Parent group: Longirostres

facts.statement: Jiangxisuchus is classified as a reptile.
facts.quote: Class: Reptilia

facts.statement: The genus Jiangxisuchus was named by Li and colleagues in 2019.
facts.quote: PBDB name: Jiangxisuchus (genus), Li et al. 2019

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Jiangxisuchus is Jiangxisuchus nankangensis.
facts.quote: Type species: Jiangxisuchus nankangensis

facts.statement: Jiangxisuchus lived between 72.2 and 66 million years ago during the Maastrichtian stage.
facts.quote: Time range: Maastrichtian to Maastrichtian (72.2 to 66 million years ago)

facts.statement: Eurycephalosuchus, a close relative of Jiangxisuchus, is characterized by a very short snout.
facts.quote: One of them was a close relative of Jiangxisuchus, the very short-snouted orientalosuchin Eurycephalosuchus

rejected.quote: The type and only known specimen of the animal, consisting of the skull, parts of the lower jaw, some partial vertebrae, ribs and osteoderms, is held at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology in Beijing.
